source_text: 1. Szniorum enim ipsorum traditio, quam ex Lege observare fingebant, contraria erat Legi date per Moysem. Propter hoc et Esaias ait: Caupones tui miscent vinwm aqua; ostendens quod austero Dei preecepto miscerent seniores aquatam traditionem, id est, aggredientes adulteram legem, et contrariam Legi, sicut et Dominus fecit manifestum, dicens eis: Quare vos transgredimint preceptum Dei propter traditionem vestram? Non solum autem per preevaricationem frustrati sunt Legem Dei, miscentes vinum aqua; sed et suam legem e contrario statuerunt, In qua quedam quidem quee usque adhuc Pharisaica yocatur. auferunt, queedam vero addunt, queedam autem, quemadmodum quibus utuntur singulariter magistri volunt, interpretantur ; eorum: quas traditiones volentes vindicare, Legi Dei instituenti eos ad adventum Christi non subjecti esse voluerunt; sed et Dominum arguebant in sabbatis curantem, quod quidem sicut preeLex non prohibebat. Etenim ipsi secundum aliquid circumcidentes hominem in sabbato; se autem ipsos non redarguebant, per traditionem et preedictam Pharisaicam legem transgredientes preeceptum Dei, et preeceptum Legis non habentes, id est dilectionem que est erga Deum. 2. Quoniam autem hoc primum et maximum praceptum est, Isequens autem erga proximum, Dominus docuit, totam legem et prophetas pendere dicens ex ipsis preceptis. Et ipse autem aliud majus hoc pret, non detulit: sed hoc ipsum renovavit suis discipulis, jubens eis Deum diligere ex toto corde, et cteros quemadmodum se. Si autem ab alio descendisset Patre, nunquam ex Lege primo et summo usus esset preecepto, sed utique omnimodo eniteretur majus hoe a perfecto Patre deferre, non eo uti quod a Deo Legis fuisset datum. Et Paulus autem: Adimpletio, Legis dilectio: et omnibus czeteris evacuatis, manere fidem, spem, dilectionem ; majorem autem esse omnium dilectionem: et Heque agnitionem sine dilectione que est erga Deum prestare aliquid ; neque mysteriorum comprehensionem neque fidem neque prophetiam, sed omnia vacua et frustra esse sine dilectione: dilectionem vero perficere perfectum hominem; et eum qui diligit: Deum esse perfectum, et in hoc evo et in futuro. Nunquam enim desinimus diligentes Deum; sed quanto plus eum intuiti fuerimus, tanto plus eum diligimus. 1. In Lege igitur et in Evangelio cum sit primum et maximum preeceptum, diligere Dominum Deum ex toto corde; dehine simile illi, diligere proximum sicut seipsum: unus et idem ostenditur Legis et Evangelii conditor. Consummatze enim vitee preecepta in utroque Testamento cum sint eadem, eundem ostenderunt Deum: qui particularia quidem preecepta apta utrisque preecepit ; sed eminentiora et summa, sine quibus salvari non est, in utroque eadem suasit. Quem autem non confundat Dominus, ostendens non ab altero Deo esse Legem, sic dicens eis qui a se docebantur, et discipulis: Super cathedram Moysi sederunt scribe: et Phariswi. Omnia itaque quecunque dixerint vobis, custodite et Jacite ; secundum autem opera eorum nolite facere: dicunt enim et non faciunt. Alligant eniin sarcinas graves, et tmponunt super humeros hominum; ipsi autem nec digito quidem volunt eas movere. Non ergo eam Legem, que est per Moysem data, incusabat, quam adhuce salvis Hierosolymis suadebat fieri; sed illos redarguebat, quod verba quidem Legis enuntiarent, essent autem sine dilectione, et propter hoc injusti in Deum et in proximos exstiterunt. Quemadmodum et Esaias ait: Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me. Frustra autem colunt me, docentes doctrinas et preecepta hominum. Non per Moysem datam Legem preecepta hominum, sed traditiones sorum, quas finxerant, quas vindicantes frustrabantur Legem Dei, et propter hoe nee Verbo ejus subjecti sunt. Hoc enim est quod et a Paulo dicitur de istis: Ignorantes enim justitiam Dei, et suam justitiam volentes statuere, justitie Dei non sunt subjecti. Finis Legis Christus ad justitiam omni credenti. Et quomodo finis Legis Christus, si non et initium ejus esset? Qui enim finem intulit, hic et initium operatus est; et ipse est qui dicit Moysi : Videns vidi vexationem populi mei qui est in A2gypto, et descendi ut eruam eos: ab initio assuetus Verbum Dei ascendere et descendere, propter salutem eorum qui male haberent. 2. Quoniam autem Lex preedocuit hominem sequi oportere Christum, ipse facit manifestum ei qui interrogavit, quid faciens vitam seternam heereditaret, sic respondens: Si vis in vitam introire, custodi preecepta. Illo autem interrogante, Qua? rursus Non mechaberis, non occides, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium reddes, honora patrem et matrem, et diliges proximum tanquam teipsum; velut gradus proponens preecepta Legis introitus in vitam, volentibus sequi eum: quee uni tum dicens, omnibus dicebat. Ille autem cum dixisset: Omnia feci, (et forte non fecerat, nam utique non diceretur ei, Custodi pracepta,) arguens Dominus cupiditatem ejus, dixit ei: Si vis perfectus esse, vade, vende omnia que habes, et divide pauperibus, et veni, sequere me; Apostolorum partem promittens eis, qui sic fecerint: et non alterum Deum Patrem annuntiabat eis qui sequebantur eum, preeter eum qui ab initio a Lege annuntiatus est; nec alium Filium, nec matrem, Enthymesin Zonis, qui fuit in passione et in defectione; nee triginta AZonum plenitudinem, que vacua et inconstans ostensa est; nec eam fabulam quz a reliquis heereticis ficta est; sed docebat, ut facerent preecepta que ab initio praecepit Deus, et ut veterem cupiditatem per opera bona solverent, et sequerentur Christum. Quoniam autem ea que possidentur pauperibus divisa, solutionem faciunt preeteritee cupiditatis, Zacchzeus fecit manifestum: Ecce, dicens, dimidium ex bonis meis do pauperibus, et si cujus quid fraudavi, reddo quadruplum.
pass_a_gloss: For the tradition of the elders themselves, which they pretended to observe from the Law, was contrary to the Law given through Moses. Because of this, Isaiah also says: Your wine merchants mix wine with water; showing that they mixed the austere command of God with the watery tradition, that is, they approached an adulterous law, and one contrary to the Law, just as the Lord made clear, saying to them: Why do you transgress the command of God because of your tradition? Not only were they frustrated by the Law of God through prevarication, mixing wine with water, but they also established their own law in opposition, in which some things are indeed taken away, which are still called Pharisaic, and some things are added, and some things are interpreted in the way the singular teachers wish; these traditions they wanted to defend, not being subject to the Law of God, which institutes them for the coming of Christ; but they also accused the Lord of healing on the Sabbath, which the Law did not prohibit. For they themselves circumcised a man on the Sabbath; but they did not accuse themselves, transgressing the command of God through tradition and the aforementioned Pharisaic law, and not having the command of the Law, that is, the love which is towards God. Because this is the first and greatest commandment, and the second is towards the neighbor, the Lord taught that the whole Law and the prophets depend on these commandments. And He Himself did not introduce another commandment greater than this, but rather renewed this one for His disciples, commanding them to love God with all their heart, and others as themselves. If, however, He had come from another Father, He would never have used the first and greatest commandment from the Law, but would have brought a greater one from the perfect Father, not using what was given by the God of the Law. And Paul also says: The fulfillment of the Law is love; and when all else is emptied, faith, hope, and love remain; and the greatest of all is love; and knowledge without love towards God is of no use; nor is the comprehension of mysteries, nor faith, nor prophecy, but all are empty and useless without love; but love perfects the perfect man; and he who loves is perfect towards God, both in this age and in the future. For we never cease loving God; but the more we have seen Him, the more we love Him. In the Law, therefore, and in the Gospel, since the first and greatest commandment is to love the Lord God with all one's heart, and then to love one's neighbor as oneself, the same God is shown to be the author of the Law and the Gospel. For the commandments of the perfect life in both Testaments, since they are the same, show the same God; who indeed gave particular commandments suitable for both, but the more eminent and greatest, without which one cannot be saved, are the same in both. But the Lord, showing that the Law is not from another God, says to those who were taught by Him, and to His disciples: The scribes and the Pharisees sit on the chair of Moses; therefore, observe and do all that they tell you; but do not do as they do, for they say and do not do. For they bind heavy burdens and lay them on men's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them even with a finger. Therefore, He did not condemn the Law given through Moses, which He still advised to be observed in Jerusalem; but He accused them of speaking the words of the Law, yet being without love, and therefore being unjust towards God and their neighbors. Just as Isaiah says: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; they worship me in vain, teaching the doctrines and commandments of men. For they did not follow the Law given through Moses, but their own traditions, which they had invented, and by defending these, they frustrated the Law of God, and therefore were not subject to His Word. For Paul also says of them: For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God. The end of the Law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes. And how can Christ be the end of the Law if He is not also its beginning? For He who brought the end also brought the beginning; and He is the one who says to Moses: Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have come down to deliver them; from the beginning, the Word of God is accustomed to ascend and descend for the salvation of those who are afflicted. Because the Law had previously taught man to follow Christ, He makes it clear to the one who asked what he should do to inherit eternal life, responding thus: If you want to enter into life, keep the commandments. And when he asked, Which ones? He replied again: Do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself; as if proposing the commandments of the Law as steps for entering into life for those who want to follow Him; and what He said to one, He said to all. But when he said, I have done all these things, (and perhaps he had not done them, for it would not have been said to him, Keep the commandments,) the Lord, accusing his cupidity, said to him: If you want to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and come, follow me; promising the part of the Apostles to those who do so; and He did not announce another God the Father to those who followed Him, except the one who was announced from the beginning by the Law; nor another Son, nor a mother, nor the thirty Aeons, which were shown to be empty and inconstant; nor the fable which was invented by the other heretics; but He taught that they should do the commandments that God had commanded from the beginning, and that they should solve their old cupidity through good works, and follow Christ. Because the things that are possessed, when divided among the poor, make a solution for past cupidity, Zacchaeus made it clear, saying: Behold, I give half of my goods to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone, I will repay fourfold.

bible_refs.note: Quare vos transgredimini preceptum Dei propter traditionem vestram
Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me
Finis Legis Christus ad justitiam omni credenti

pass_b_english: The elders' own tradition, which they pretended to derive from the Law, stood in direct opposition to the Law that Moses delivered. That is why Isaiah cries out, 'Your wine merchants mix wine with water' (Isaiah 29:13), exposing how they diluted the austere command of God with a watery tradition — in effect, substituting an adulterous law that contradicted the true Law. The Lord Himself made the same charge: 'Why do you transgress the command of God for the sake of your tradition?' (Matthew 15:3). They did not merely frustrate God's Law by this prevarication, mixing wine with water; they also erected a counter-law of their own. In it, some commandments still recognized as Pharisaic are removed, others are added, and still others are twisted to suit the whims of individual teachers. They clung to these traditions precisely to avoid submitting to the Law of God, which was designed to prepare them for Christ's coming. They even accused the Lord of healing on the Sabbath, though the Law never forbade such mercy. After all, they themselves circumcised a man on the Sabbath without self-condemnation, yet they violated God's commandment through their tradition and Pharisaic code, lacking the very heart of the Law: love toward God.

Because love of God is the first and greatest commandment, and love of neighbor the second, Jesus taught that the whole Law and the Prophets hang on these two (Matthew 22:37–40). He did not introduce a new, higher commandment; He renewed this same one for His disciples, ordering them to love God with all their heart and their neighbor as themselves. Had He come from a different Father, He would never have appealed to the Law's first and greatest commandment, but would have brought a superior one from that perfect Father, rather than using what the God of the Law had given. Paul agrees: 'Love is the fulfillment of the Law' (Romans 13:10). When everything else is stripped away, faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love (1 Corinthians 13:13). Knowledge without love toward God profits nothing; neither the grasp of mysteries, nor faith, nor prophecy avails — all are empty and futile without love. Love perfects the perfect person, and the one who loves is perfect toward God, both in this age and in the age to come. We never cease loving God; the more we behold Him, the more we love Him.

Therefore, since the Law and the Gospel alike set the first and greatest commandment as loving the Lord God with all your heart, and the second as loving your neighbor as yourself, the same God is revealed as the Author of both. The commandments of perfect life are identical in the two Testaments, and they point to one and the same God. He gave particular commandments suited to each era, but the supreme and essential ones — without which no one can be saved — He kept the same in both. The Lord shames those who claim the Law comes from another God when He tells His disciples, 'The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat; so practice and observe whatever they tell you, but not what they do, for they preach but do not practice. They bind heavy burdens and lay them on men's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with so much as a finger' (Matthew 23:2–4). He was not condemning the Law given through Moses — which He still urged people to keep while Jerusalem stood — but indicting those who recited the Law's words while lacking love, thereby becoming unjust toward both God and neighbor. As Isaiah says, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men' (Isaiah 29:13). They were not following the Law of Moses, but their own invented traditions; by defending these, they nullified God's Law and refused submission to His Word. Paul says of them, 'For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness' (Romans 10:3). 'Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes' (Romans 10:4). And how could Christ be the Law's end if He were not also its beginning? The One who brought the end also wrought the beginning. He is the One who said to Moses, 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have come down to deliver them' (Exodus 3:7–8). From the start, the Word of God has been accustomed to ascend and descend for the salvation of the afflicted.

Since the Law had already taught that man must follow Christ, Jesus makes this plain to the man who asked what he must do to inherit eternal life. 'If you would enter life, keep the commandments,' He replied. When the man asked, 'Which ones?' Jesus listed them: 'You shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself' (Matthew 19:17–19) — offering the Law's commandments as steps toward life for all who would follow Him. What He said to one, He said to all. The man claimed, 'I have kept all these' (though perhaps he had not, or Jesus would not have told him to keep the commandments). Exposing his covetousness, the Lord said, 'If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess, give to the poor, and come, follow me' (Matthew 19:21), promising a share in the apostles' lot to those who do so. He did not proclaim a different God the Father to His followers than the One announced from the beginning by the Law; nor a different Son; nor a 'mother' or the thirty Aeons, shown to be empty and unstable; nor the fable concocted by other heretics. Instead, He taught them to do the commandments God gave from the beginning, to undo their ancient covetousness through good works, and to follow Christ. Zacchaeus demonstrated that distributing possessions to the poor satisfies the debt of past covetousness: 'Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold' (Luke 19:8).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the nuances of the Pharisaic traditions and the theological arguments regarding the continuity of the Law and the Gospel. Scripture citations in Pass B (e.g., Matthew 15:3, Romans 13:10, Exodus 3:7-8) are correctly identified based on the Latin content. The title 'Love of God and Neighbor' correctly names the thought of the chapter.
